To angle for something means to try to get what you want, but indirectly — through hints, flattery, clever maneuvering, or subtle behavior — rather than simply asking for it openly and directly.

Think of it this way: instead of walking through a door, the person is looking for a window.
Where the Phrase Comes From (And Why It Matters)

The phrase comes from fishing. The old word for a fishhook was an angle, and fishing with a hook and line was called angling. An angler doesn't grab a fish with their bare hands — they use bait, patience, and skill to lure the fish into coming to them.

This image was so powerful that people started using it to describe human behavior. Just like a fisherman uses indirect means to catch a fish, a person who angles for something uses indirect means to get what they want. They set the bait, wait, and hope the other person "bites."

This origin is not just a fun fact — it is the key to remembering the phrase forever. Every time you hear "angle for," picture a fisherman patiently dangling bait in the water, hoping to pull something in without ever touching it directly.

This is the heart of the phrase. If someone angles for something, they are not asking for it plainly. They are working around the sides to get there.

Here is the clearest contrast to fix it in your mind:

  • Direct: "Please give me a raise."
  • Angling for a raise: Constantly mentioning how hard you work, how long your hours are, and how your colleague at another company earns so much more — all without ever saying "give me a raise."

The person's real goal is the same in both cases, but the approach is completely different.

Example 1 — Angling for a compliment:
Your friend shows you a painting they made and says, "I don't know... I'm probably not very good at art. This probably looks terrible, right?"
They are not really asking for your honest opinion. They are angling for a compliment — hoping you'll say "No, it's wonderful!"

Example 2 — Angling for an invitation:
A coworker says, "Oh, I heard you're having a dinner party this weekend. That sounds so fun. I love dinner parties. I haven't been to one in ages..."
They haven't asked to come. But they are clearly angling for an invitation.

Example 3 — Angling for sympathy:
Someone keeps talking about how exhausted and stressed they are, sighing loudly, and looking sad — not because they want advice, but because they want you to comfort them and say "Oh, you poor thing."
They are angling for sympathy.

Example 4 — Angling for information:
A journalist keeps asking a politician questions that slowly circle closer and closer to a sensitive topic, trying to get them to slip up and reveal something.
The journalist is angling for a confession or a revealing statement.
The Tone: Slightly Cunning, Sometimes Negative

It is important to know that "angle for" carries a mildly negative or critical tone in most situations. It suggests that the person is being a little crafty, sneaky, or calculating. When you say someone is "angling for" something, you are subtly implying that their behavior is not entirely straightforward or honest.

However, the negativity is not always strong. Sometimes it is used with gentle humor or mild disapproval, not harsh judgment. It depends on the context.

For example:

  • "She's obviously angling for the lead role in the play" — this sounds slightly critical, like she's scheming.
  • "He's been angling for a compliment all evening" — this sounds more amused than angry.

The key thing to remember: it always suggests the person is not being fully open or direct about what they want.

"Angle for" is a phrasal verb. It is always followed by a noun or noun phrase — the thing the person is trying to get.

The structure is: angle for + [something wanted]

You can use it in any tense:

  • She is angling for a promotion. (present continuous — most common)
  • He angled for her sympathy all evening. (past)
  • They have been angling for that contract for months. (present perfect continuous)
  • Stop angling for compliments. (imperative)

The present continuous form ("is/was angling for") is by far the most natural and common, because the phrase describes an ongoing, deliberate behavior — not a single moment.

These are the most frequent combinations you will encounter:

  • Angle for a compliment — fishing for praise
  • Angle for a promotion — maneuvering to move up at work
  • Angle for an invitation — hinting to be included
  • Angle for sympathy — trying to get people to feel sorry for you
  • Angle for attention — behaving in ways to make people notice you
  • Angle for information — trying to get someone to reveal something
  • Angle for a deal / contract — strategically working to secure a business agreement
  • Angle for a position / role — trying to land a job or part in something

Knowing related phrases helps you understand "angle for" more deeply by seeing what it is close to and different from:

"Fish for" — Almost identical in meaning and tone. "Fishing for compliments" and "angling for compliments" mean the same thing. Both come from fishing. You can use them interchangeably in most cases. "Fish for" might feel slightly more casual.

"Hint at" — To hint at something means to suggest it indirectly. Angling for is a broader activity that can include hinting, but also involves actions, maneuvering, and behavior — not just words.

"Drop hints" — Similar to hinting, but specifically about letting small clues fall into conversation. Again, this is one tool someone might use while angling for something.

"Maneuver for" — This is more formal and suggests a more deliberate, strategic effort, often in professional or political contexts. Less casual than "angle for."

"Be after" — This means wanting something but does not necessarily imply the indirectness. "He's after a raise" just means he wants one. "He's angling for a raise" means he's working toward it sneakily.

One Final Example to Bring It All Together

Imagine you are at a party. Your friend spent weeks planning a trip and wants you to join. Instead of saying "Come with me on this trip," they spend the whole evening saying things like: "It's going to be so much fun... I just wish I had someone to share it with... You mentioned you needed a vacation... It would be perfect for you..."

Your friend is angling for you to offer to join the trip — trying to get you there through a side door, not the front one.

That is exactly what "angle for" means. Every time.
